Chapter 3: Wrestling with Belief in a Secular World
Leaving home and stepping into the wider world—it’s a big shift, isn’t it? Suddenly, all the comfort and routine you grew up with feel a little distant. College classrooms and busy city streets don’t always make room for the language of faith. When you’re surrounded by people who prize reason and skepticism, it’s surprisingly easy to let those old beliefs slip away. Maybe you start by skipping Mass once or twice, or you forget to pray at night. Before long, those rituals from your childhood can seem like they belong to someone else, or maybe even another lifetime.
But in this new environment, the questions only get sharper. Can you really believe in something you can’t prove? Is there room for faith in a world that’s all about science and logic? Some folks will tell you, absolutely not. They find their meaning in art, in friendships, or just in learning new things. But for others, losing that sense of faith isn’t freeing—it leaves a kind of emptiness, like something important has gone missing.
Picture this: It’s late, and a young professional is walking home after a long day. He passes by churches, all closed up and dark, and he suddenly remembers what it felt like back in his old parish—the warmth, the sense of community, the feeling that he truly belonged. Now, in a city full of strangers and noise, he feels a deep longing. And it’s not just about what he believes. It’s about wanting to feel at home, to find a place in a world that sometimes seems cold or indifferent.
The struggle between faith and doubt? It’s rarely simple. Most of us bounce between feeling certain and questioning everything—sometimes all in a single day. There are moments when those old prayers come back out of nowhere, and they actually bring comfort when you need it most. Other times, the doubts are so loud that even the rituals feel empty.
You might notice that, in conversations with friends, religion is almost never on the table. It’s easier to chat about work, or politics, or the latest TV show, than to admit you’re not sure what you believe anymore. But here’s the thing—underneath it all, a lot of us are searching for the same thing. We’re looking for meaning, for some way to make sense of the hard stuff and the happy moments.
Over time, something important becomes clear: faith and doubt aren’t really opposites. They can live side by side, shaping each other. The journey isn’t a straight line. There are setbacks, flashes of understanding, days when those old stories suddenly make sense, and days when they don’t. Most of us never find all the answers. But we do learn to live with the questions—and sometimes, there’s real peace in that search itself.
